title: Your King Comes, Humble and Riding on a Donkey
summary: The first of two burdens, or oracles, opens with the LORD's judgment moving down through Syria, Phoenicia, and Philistia, while he guards his own house. Then Jerusalem is called to rejoice at the arrival of her king, righteous and victorious, humble and riding on a donkey, who will end war and speak peace to the nations. God promises to free his prisoners because of the blood of his covenant, to fight for his people against the sons of Greece, and to save them as a shepherd saves his flock.
story: With chapter 9 the book changes voice. The dated visions and sermons of chapters 1 to 8 give way to undated poetry under the heading burden, or oracle. The rebuilding of the temple and the names of Joshua and Zerubbabel disappear, and the horizon widens to God's final victory over the nations and the coming of Israel's king. The promises of chapters 1 to 8, that God would return to Jerusalem and the nations would come to him, are now described as a divine march of conquest ending in a king's entry into his city. The chapter opens the first of two oracle collections (chapters 9 to 11 and 12 to 14), and it contains the verse the Gospels would quote at Jesus's entry into Jerusalem.
historical:
The route in verses 1-7 names real places. Hadrach was a city and region in northern Syria, known from Assyrian records as Hatarikka, near Hamath on the Orontes River. Damascus was the chief city of Aram, south of Hamath. Tyre and Sidon were the great Phoenician port cities on the coast; Tyre was built partly on an island and was famous for its wealth and its strength. Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron, and Ashdod were four of the five cities of the Philistines on the southern coast. The line of march runs from north to south, ending at Judah's border.

When this oracle was written is debated (see the introduction). Many scholars note that the route resembles Alexander the Great's campaign of 333 and 332 BC, when after defeating the Persians at Issus he moved down the coast, took Tyre after a seven-month siege, and then took Gaza, and they date the chapter to that time or read it as describing it. Others, who hold that Zechariah wrote these chapters, place them in the early fifth century BC, when Greeks and Persians were already at war (the Persian invasions of Greece in 490 and 480 BC), or read the march as a stylized picture drawn from older Assyrian campaigns through the same region. The mention of Greece in verse 13 (Hebrew Javan, the Ionian Greeks) fits either setting, since Greeks traded and fought across the eastern Mediterranean throughout the Persian period.
cultural:
Kings in the ancient Near East normally went to war in chariots or on horseback. The donkey, though, was not a lowly animal in every setting: it was a common mount for travel and for people of standing in peacetime, and in Israel's history it had royal associations. The judges' sons rode donkeys (Judges 10:4), and David had Solomon ride his own mule to his anointing (1 Kings 1:33-38). Jacob's blessing of Judah speaks of the ruler tying his donkey's colt to the vine (Genesis 49:10-11). A king riding a donkey rather than a war horse came in peace, not conquest, and verse 10 makes the point by removing chariots and war horses from Israel altogether.

The blood from their mouths and abominations between their teeth (verse 7) refer to food forbidden in Israel's law, meat eaten with its blood (Leviticus 17:10-14) and unclean foods offered in pagan worship. Removing them means the Philistines will be cleansed and join God's people. Ekron will be like the Jebusites, the original inhabitants of Jerusalem, who were absorbed into Israel after David took the city (2 Samuel 5:6-9). The sprinkling bowls and the corners of the altar in verse 15 are pictures from temple sacrifice, where priests caught blood in bowls and splashed it on the altar's corners.
literary: The chapter is poetry, with the parallelism typical of Hebrew verse: each line is echoed or advanced by the next (rejoice greatly, O Daughter of Zion; shout in triumph, O Daughter of Jerusalem). It has three movements. Verses 1-8 are a march of divine judgment ending with God guarding his house. Verses 9-10 are the center, a royal proclamation announcing the king. Verses 11-17 are a promise of release and holy war, ending with a picture of plenty and beauty. The speaker shifts between God (I will cut off, I will release) and the prophet speaking about God (the LORD will appear over them), a common feature of prophetic poetry. Verse 10 echoes Psalm 72:8, a royal psalm about the ideal king whose rule extends from sea to sea.

outline.t: The LORD against Hadrach, Damascus, Hamath, Tyre, and Sidon
The Philistines humbled and cleansed; God guards his house
Your King comes, humble and riding on a donkey
Prisoners of hope released by the blood of the covenant
The LORD appears, fights, and saves his flock

doctrines.note: Verse 9 describes the coming king as righteous, victorious (literally saved or delivered), and humble. He ends war, speaks peace to the nations, and rules to the ends of the earth. The combination of gentleness and universal rule is distinctive.

God frees his prisoners because of the blood of my covenant (verse 11), recalling the blood Moses sprinkled on the people at Sinai (Exodus 24:8). Rescue flows from God's commitment sealed by blood, not from the prisoners' merit.

The chapter pictures God's rule spreading across the nations, first in judgment on proud cities and then in peace proclaimed by his king. Even the Philistines, Israel's old enemies, can become a remnant for our God.

words.note: Ani, afflicted, poor, or humble. The word often describes the oppressed poor whom God defends. Applied to the king in verse 9, it means he comes lowly, not in the pride of a conqueror. Many translations render it humble or gentle, and Matthew's Greek quotation uses a word meaning gentle.

Chamor, donkey. It was the ordinary animal of transport and farm work, and in Israel a mount of peace and sometimes of royalty. The verse repeats itself, a donkey, a colt, the foal of a donkey, in typical Hebrew parallelism, describing one animal in three ways.

Berit, covenant. A covenant was a binding commitment between two parties, often sealed with a sacrifice. The blood of my covenant in verse 11 recalls Sinai and grounds God's promise to release his people from the waterless pit.

Tiqvah, hope, from a root meaning to wait or, in some uses, a cord. The phrase prisoners of hope in verse 12 is striking: those still bound are held by hope, called to return to their stronghold, God himself.

christ: Matthew and John both quote verse 9 when Jesus rides into Jerusalem at the start of his final week (Matthew 21:4-5; John 12:14-15), and all four Gospels describe the event. Jesus arranged the ride himself (Mark 11:1-7), which makes the act a deliberate claim: he enters the city as its king, but as the humble king of Zechariah's promise rather than as a warrior. John adds that the disciples did not understand this at first, but remembered it after Jesus was glorified (John 12:16). The phrase the blood of my covenant in verse 11 is also echoed at the Last Supper, when Jesus called the cup my blood of the covenant, poured out for many (Mark 14:24), words that go back first to Exodus 24:8. The peace the king proclaims to the nations is the peace Paul says Christ preached to those far away and those near (Ephesians 2:17). The chapter's vision of a universal reign is not yet fully seen; the New Testament places its completion at Christ's return.

hard.q: Why does a chapter about a king of peace also celebrate violent victory over the nations?
hard.a: The chapter holds both pictures side by side: the humble king who removes the war horse and speaks peace (verses 9-10), and the LORD who makes Judah his bow and his people like a warrior's sword, drinking and roaring (verses 13-15). Readers are right to feel the tension. Several points help. The warfare is God's own action against the powers that oppressed his people, not a license for human aggression; the victory comes as God appears over them, with lightning and trumpet, in the language of a storm theophany. The judgment also has a purpose beyond destruction: even the Philistines become a remnant for our God (verse 7). Jewish interpreters have often read the violence as describing a historical deliverance, and Christian interpreters have commonly read it through the cross and the final judgment, in which Christ conquers evil and establishes peace. The New Testament keeps the same pairing: the lamb who was slain is also the one who judges and makes war in righteousness (Revelation 5:6; 19:11). The chapter asks readers to hold both, and to note that the final word of the king is peace.

questions: What does it tell you about God's kind of power that his king chooses a donkey rather than a war horse?
Prisoners of hope are still bound but held by hope. Where are you waiting as one of them?
Even the Philistines are pictured becoming a clan in Judah. Who are the people you find hardest to imagine being welcomed by God?
